text: Done. Report

**What I found:** the 50-state picture collapses to four ti
ers. **Illinois is the only genuinely dangerous state** — sole broad private right of action, $1,000/$5,000 per
person plus fees. **Texas** is AG-only but counts one violation per resident at up to $25k
(the math behind Meta's $1.4B). **Colorado** is strictest of the
~20 comprehensive-privacy states and applies with no volume threshold. **Washington** looks mild until you add My Health My Data,
which does carry a private right. **Portland OR** bans private facial recognition outright ($1k/day, private right) and **NYC** has a private right — both prob

ably out of scope for a remote app, but Portland needs counsel's read.

**Recommendation: don't geofence.**
Since SB 2979 (Aug 2024), Illinois accepts an e-signed release and damages accrue once per person rather than
per scan — so one BIPA+Colorado-grade flow over-satisfies all 50 states and costs you a consent screen plus a

deletion job.

Four non-negotiables before first collection: pre-capture e-signed release stating purpose and storage term; publicly posted retention/

destruction policy; automated deletion (delete on successful verify, 1-year hard cap); never sell or share.

The tree now has 12 sub
tasks — 4 research tasks done with findings in their descriptions, 8 open and
mostly human: the launch-posture decision, counsel review, publishing the policy, the vendor retention question, the consent screen
, the deletion job, and a non-biometric fallback. I also spun off auto-renewal/click-to-cancel for the subscription side — unrelated to biometrics,
but it'll bite at launch.
